subject: Copywriting
subcategory: The Science of Storytelling in Ads
title: The Everyman Character

hook.text: Subway's Jared lost 245 lbs eating sandwiches. He wasn't a model. He was a regular guy—and that's why it worked.

buildup.text: The Everyman archetype is relatable because audiences see themselves. If he can do it, so can I. That's the logic.

discovery.text: Dove's 'Real Beauty' campaign used everyday women instead of supermodels. Sales jumped 700% in the first year.

twist.text: The Everyman fails when the audience suspects staging. Authenticity must be real—scripted 'regular people' feel fake.

climax.text: User-generated content is the ultimate Everyman. Real customers sharing real results with no script and no budget.

punchline.text: Regular people sell better than celebrities. Relatability wins.

quiz.question: How much did Dove's 'Real Beauty' campaign boost sales?

details.summary: The Everyman character — an ordinary person facing ordinary problems — is advertising's most effective protagonist. When the audience sees someone just like them in an ad, identification is instant. The Everyman's success with the product feels achievable, not aspirational and out of reach.
details.whyItMatters: Celebrity endorsements grab attention, but Everyman characters drive conversion because they trigger the thought 'if this regular person can do it, so can I.' Relatability is more persuasive than aspiration for most products.
takeaways: Ordinary characters create stronger audience identification than celebrities
The Everyman's success feels achievable and replicable
Specificity makes Everyman characters feel real, not generic

faq.question: When is an Everyman character more effective than a celebrity?
faq.answer: For products where the audience needs to believe they can achieve the same results. Weight loss, financial tools, learning platforms, and everyday consumer goods benefit from Everyman characters because the message is 'this person is just like you and they succeeded.'

faq.question: How do you make an Everyman character compelling?
faq.answer: Make them specific, not generic. A 'busy mom from Ohio who works two jobs and still found time to learn guitar' is infinitely more compelling than 'a regular person.' Specific details — name, location, circumstances — transform a type into a person the audience cares about.
